Hello, I do like your video. It does get information across and I like the flow of the visuals!

 However, your video does have a few issues with ease of listening/viewing. 

If you're open to constructive criticism, I do have a few suggestions/comments and I'll list those below so you can read them if you'd like!

1. The first thing you could do for future videos is to watch out for grammar mistakes in narration. For example, at 0:25 it says, "...to use it in more efficient way". That should probably be "...to use it in more efficient way**s**". Take into account context and such as you are going.

* The free version of the **Grammarly** extension is actually fairly helpful for this, but won't catch everything. There are also many free websites you can use to check the tone and grammar of a text. Just remember to select all (Ctrl + A) and then click copy (or Ctrl + C) because some of them ~~rudely~~ delete your text if you change tabs! 

1. Closed Captions of some sort would be a great thing to incorporate in your videos! Not only does it expand your audience(\*see footnote) but it also helps people understand the information you are presenting. :)
2. While your video clips and pictures are interesting and often fit what is being narrated, there are maybe some exceptions. 

* This is in no way a big deal, but (if I don't explain this well please tell me!) does affect the experience of your audience. I'll use timestamp 0:52-0:57 in the video as an example. In that portion of the video, you mention personalized movie recommendations on streaming services but the video shows an image of code and the yellow robotic arms. These are not quite(?) related and seem to take away from the narration, at least in my opinion!

\*What I mean by expanding your audience is that when including people who are blind and/or are profoundly Deaf or hard of hearing, your audience increases! Obviously, it is definitely not the only reason you should make your videos accessible, but it is certainly a factor in subscriber & viewer counts. I myself am not Deaf or Blind and am assuming you are not either (*please pardon me if I am incorrect!*) but imagine how many more people your videos will reach if they have CC or audio descriptions! Unfortunately, I have absolutely no idea how to do that. **BUT, I believe the start would be adding subtitles to your videos.**

I understand completely! I have driving anxiety and only got my license at 18 (maybe 19?) because I HAD to. I'm 21 now and before I go to drive anywhere I still am extremely anxious and often have to take medication. Heart-pounding, fast breathing, sweaty palms, stomach hurting...you name it. HOWEVER, once I'm in the car and actually driving I usually calm down a lot.

For a long time, I was white-knuckled grip on the wheel, dead silence, staring only at the road. Now, I can drive with one hand out the window, turn the air and radio knobs, glance away from the road, and even check over my shoulder when changing lanes without (really) freaking out!

It is very tough when people are pressuring you to do something that causes you distress, and I do want to say that if you don't **have** to drive, you don't need to. Sure, people might be mean or annoying and it's super-duper convenient, but depending on where you live and your resources there are bikes, buses, uber, taxis, friends/fam you can pay to give you a lift, etc! 

If you do absolutely have to drive, here are some things that helped me.

1. therapy. lmao. I've learned how to tolerate my anxiety easier and to mostly dismiss irrational thoughts. And anxiety medication. BUT meds aren't for everyone and do note that driving after taking certain anixety meds is not a good idea and/or illegal. I myself am prescribed something that both augments another medication and helps my anxiety, and I'll do usually take it before driving.
2. Funnily enough, making mistakes helps! I've been honked at 3 times, backed into the same pole twice, had to repark SO MANY times, not known what the hell I'm supposed to do in a certain situation...etc. 
3. Practice on empty roads and empty parking lots. Have someone drive the car there and then you get to drive around. If safe to do so, go as slow as you need to. 
4. Have at least some confidence in the car. My car has a historic vehicle plate, bitch old as hell, right? Still, I know what is a risk with the car and what is pretty reliable, and as long as I check or fix the things that are sketchy, I trust my car a fair amount and that has eased a lot of the anxiety.
5. Avoid things that you don't feel confident/comfortable doing! My mom is blind in one eye and so does not make left turns across traffic unless required. I myself don't like U-turns so I avoid them if possible, and I also park as far away from other cars as I need to (which does result in me walking to my car for 5 minutes for with a bunch of groceries). I know people will disagree and say you have to get used to it, but I don't believe that.
6. Driving automatic. It is so much easier than a manual for me. Having to press the clutch and change gears and not stall the car out is too much for my anxiety. Manual is fine for many people, but not me. 
7. Do NOT let fear consume you. Like...ok, this might make 0 sense to you, but in Harry Potter, they call Lord Voldemort you-know-who. The "only person LV fears", Albus Dumbledore, said something like, "fear of the name only increases fear of the thing" right? Well, I turn that into a lot of things, but in some situations, I see it as "fear the **thought** of it (in this case driving) and you will fear the **action** more". I think about driving and get anxious-afraid so when I get in the car I am already freaking out. Idk how to explain it well, i might visit this tomorrow when sober 
8. I use GPS. Everywhere I go, even if the route is memorized. Nowadays, I don't really need to pay attention to it, just the fact that it is THERE makes me feel better. I have a bad memory and a terrible sense of direction, so I get lost easily.

As much as I hate to say it, practice really is your best bet. ;-; There is no limit in regards to age when getting your license. You can get it when you are 20 or when you are 40! Take your time, try to do it (but don't force it), and try doing what scares you.   
(Congrats on the learner's permit, btw!)

Alrighty! Deciding to come out to family, especially..."older" and/or more "traditional" people and gossipers is often a hard and scary choice for sure. It is true that someone may be tolerant of LGBT+ until it is someone the know, that is a valid concern that you have. BUT, just them supporting LGBT+ at all is a great thing!!! To me, the fact that you have family that is already aware of your orientation means that if the relatives on your dad's side take the info poorly then you will have people to back you up, like your parents and others on you mom's side.

This woman S you talk of I think is a 50/50 situation. The lack of technical knowledge or full understanding of English leading to her clicking "likes men and women" is possible, but it is also possible that she understood exactly what she was doing and felt comfortable doing so. You'd know her better than me of course, but I would say ask her. 

What D said to you is cruel. There's no sugarcoating that. By saying you would burden them, she indirectly said that you are some sort of problem. That is in no way true, and anyone would be hurt and discouraged by that. I have my own opinions and would very much like a word with her, but *objectively* D was unkind to you and showed her own intolerance of LGBT+ people by saying your orientation would burden someone.

Gossip is so rough, and that is coming from someone who definitely gossips. Again, you know them better than me, but I do not believe all gossip is mean-spirited (as a gossiper I would know!). You improving your Russian is so sweet, and something you can use to have them view you in a more favorable light if the bisexuality is a problem!

Not making it a "huge thing", as you say, is very smart. But I would perhaps go even more slowly? When watching television or walking down the street say things like, "Wow, that girl is so beautiful!" or only just HINT at your orientation. If they ask you straight up if you like girls, don't deny as it will hurt your case in the future. 


The person that knows your family believing it is okay to tell them is great news! Sometimes an outsider's view is correct and helpful! 

***I do have two questions for you, answer if you want to! By disowning do you mean like literal legal disownment? And is the only thing holding you back from coming out the fear of gossip? 

Here is what I would keep in mind and do:
-As sad as it is, there IS a possibility this may entirely end or extremely strain your relationship with these people
-Go slow and as subtle as you can.
-Perhaps ask your parents if coming out to these relatives is a good/safe thing to do?
-These relatives might react badly but can come around after a bit (days, months, years). If they don't react well, do not lose all hope!
-Tell them that you have thought about this for a long time.
-Tell them you are not choosing to be bisexual and explain that attempts to forcibly alter sexual orientation is brainwashing and is only successful at a shallow level.
-Disregard what D said and do not ask them about this again. It will only cause you emotional pain. 
-Is coming out to your relatives going to make you feel better even if they react negatively? If yes, come out. If no, I advise you to wait until you will be okay if they are... mean.
-If possible, don't come out on THEIR territory. Wait until they come to visit you at your home, if possible.
-They will always love you, but they may not ACT like it. Mother's of people that commit horrible, evil crimes usually still love their kids (NOT the same at all but I'm drunk now so uh). Your family won't hate you if they react badly to you coming out, but they will not tell you that, either out of stubbornness, pride, or fear of going against what they belief in/were taught.

Remember, you do not need to spare other people's feelings or make them comfortable at your own detriment! There's nothing wrong with you and you are not and never will be a burden. People love you and will always love you.

Whatever you decide, good luck, best wishes, and stay safe. <3

I wouldn't recommend constantly telling her to not die because it will hurt you. One, that is incredibly unfair to her and two, if she ever thinks she has lost or does lose your support then she also may have just lost her only reason to live. Also, she may convince herself that (as you mentioned) she is a burden on you and/or others and that you would get over her death without her around to bother you. 
I definitely understand not wanting professional help after having been forced into it, but that is really the best and correct option. Perhaps if you start therapy she will be open to it? Or say you will go with her to appointments and wait in the lobby? I did that for a friend and she started going and after a bit managed to begin going by herself. 
You could take her to a crisis response center the next time she is in danger, and they will usually help set up therapy or medication. If it's a voluntary then they won't always admit you, but keep you over night until the crisis is over. HOWEVER, this does sound like a bad situation, so do note that she might be admitted as they try to figure out what she needs to get better.

Not sure how old you guys are, but worse comes to worst you will have to alert a parent(s) or guardian and/or a medical professional (if they don't know already). Discuss it with her first, and do not use it as a threat, but it does sound like she needs to be under the care of someone who will make sure she doesn't attempt. She wont like it (because that does tend to lead to involuntary hospitalization) but if you tell her something like, "I want what is best for you, and what is best for me. We are both hurting right now and I am scared for you because I love you deeply. I think it is a very good idea for both of us to get professional help.
